## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Coding agents are increasingly used to build, improve, and review scientific analyses, yet there is little evidence on what they contribute in each of these roles or on the problems they introduce. This study examined that question through a complete remote sensing analysis in which agents built the pipeline, optimised one of its methods in a sandboxed loop, and audited the plan, the literature, and the draft. The worked example estimated spring green-up in Wapusk National Park from daily MODIS imagery and found no detectable trend between 2001 and 2024, while snow-off and spring warmth together explained 77% of its year-to-year variation. The optimizer agent reduced held-out synthetic error by 6% over 33 iterations, but its improvements did not carry over to year-to-year agreement on real pixels, it reasoned directly from the benchmark generator it could read, and it gamed its score once its ideas ran out. In contrast, the auditing agents caught 20 of the 24 consequential problems recorded in the project, including an optimisation objective that would have biased the trend and a misreported variance partition. These findings suggest that, in this case, agents added more value by checking research than by optimising it, and that agentic research needs evaluators scored on the scientific estimand, benchmarks the agent cannot read, and safeguards enforced in code rather than in time.

## Introduction

Coding agents can now write analysis pipelines, propose improvements to methods, and review manuscripts. Recent systems formalise one of these roles as a loop in which an agent edits a program and a fixed evaluator decides which changes survive [@karpathy2026; @novikov2025; @chan2024]. These systems are typically judged by the score they optimise, however, rather than by whether the science improves, and there is little evidence on how the different roles an agent can play compare within a single study.

This study therefore used a complete analysis as a case study. The analysis was a pre-registered estimate of spring green-up in Wapusk National Park, Manitoba, whose caribou and nesting geese depend on the timing of fresh forage [@doiron2013; @mallory2020]. It tested three alternative hypotheses: that green-up advanced between 2001 and 2024 (H1), that later snow-off brings later green-up (H2), and that spring warmth explains variation beyond snow-off (H3). Within that analysis, the study asked three research questions:

1. **(RQ1)** What did agents contribute in each of their roles, as builder, optimizer, and auditor?
2. **(RQ2)** Did the optimizer's improvements carry over to the scientific result?
3. **(RQ3)** How did the optimizer behave under a fixed objective, and what does that behaviour imply for designing such loops?

The paper then sets out what went wrong, the challenges this approach poses for research, and the experiments most worth trying next.

## Methods

### The Research Task

Daily MOD09GA collection 6.1 reflectance [@vermote2021mod09ga] was quality masked, and NDVI [@tucker1979] was computed for 300 pixels drawn at random on the MODIS 500 m grid, 75 in each of four land-cover strata [@zanaga2022]. For each pixel-season, snow-flagged days were anchored at a dormant baseline [@beck2006; @gray2019guide], the series was smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter fitted to the upper envelope [@chen2004], and mid-green-up was taken as the day the curve reached half of its seasonal amplitude [@white1997]. Snow-off came from ERA5-Land [@munozsabater2021] and thawing degree days (TDD) from the Churchill climate station, and the trend and associations were tested with Theil–Sen slopes, Mann–Kendall tests, and nested least-squares models [@sen1968; @yue2002]. The basis for each method is documented in `docs/methods_justification.md`.

### Agent Roles

Every agent in the study was an instance of Claude Code working under the author's direction, in one of four roles (@tbl-roles).

| Role | Task | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Builder | Wrote the pipeline, pre-registration, and drafts | Full repository and data, under human direction |
| Optimizer | Improved the green-up extractor in a loop | Read the repository; edit one file; no code execution |
| Auditors | Reviewed the plan, checked the literature, refereed the draft | Read-only, with web search for the literature and referee roles |
| Harness tests | Scripted agents that deliberately broke the loop's rules | Edit any file, to test enforcement |

: Agent roles in the case study. {#tbl-roles}

### The Optimizer Loop

The optimizer could edit only `method.py`, the file containing the green-up extractor, and could read the evaluator, the benchmark generator, and a ledger of earlier attempts, but it could not run code, use the web, or read held-out data. A driver outside the agent reverted any other change, verified the evaluator's hash before and after every call, and kept a change only if its score on 1,800 synthetic seasons fell. The score was the mean error in days plus small penalties for line count and runtime. After 33 iterations, the frozen candidate was scored once on held-out synthetic seasons, including a family built from real NDVI shapes, and compared with the pre-registered method on real pixels against four entry criteria fixed in advance.

### Evaluating Contributions

Consequential problems raised during the project, and the changes they caused, were recorded by role (`results/tables/agent_contributions.csv`). After the loop, every kept version of the extractor was re-scored on held-out and real data, and each of the 33 iterations was coded by the kind of change attempted, from the optimizer's own rationale (`autoresearch/iteration_coding.csv`).

## Results

### The Worked Example

Mid-green-up averaged day of year 180 (late June) and showed no detectable trend between 2001 and 2024 (+0.03 days/yr, 95% CI −0.33 to +0.47), which does not support H1 (@fig-series). Snow-off and spring warmth supported H2 and H3: each standard deviation (15 days) of later snow-off corresponded to green-up 5.4 days later (R² = 0.52), and TDD raised the explained variance to 77%. The record can only reliably detect trends of about 0.7–0.9 days/yr, however, and the contribution of warmth depended on the temperature window.

![Annual mid-green-up from this study and from the MCD12Q2 product, with the Theil–Sen trend.](../results/figures/greenup_series.png){#fig-series}

### Contributions by Role (RQ1)

The auditing agents caught 20 of the 24 consequential problems recorded in the project, and 17 of their 20 changed a design decision or a claim (@tbl-contributions). The plan reviewer raised the most consequential of these before any code ran. The first design of the optimizer's objective would have pulled each year toward the long-term average and copied the comparison product's trend, biasing the very result the study set out to test. After the first draft, the referee found that the variance partition was misreported, that causal language contradicted the pre-registration, and that an apparent conflict with Mallory et al. [-@mallory2020] rested on a mismatched comparison. A like-for-like comparison over 2004–2016 then showed the results to be compatible. The builder introduced several of these errors itself, including a park boundary reprojected into the wrong UTM zone and a misattributed citation. The optimizer, in contrast, contributed one useful idea (iteration 8), which was not adopted under the entry rule.

| Role | Problems recorded | Changed a design or claim |
|---|---|---|
| Plan reviewer | 8 | 8 |
| Literature auditors | 6 | 3 |
| Referee | 6 | 6 |
| Harness tests and builder self-checks | 2 | 2 |
| Optimizer | 1 | 0 |
| Human author | 1 | 1 |

: Consequential problems recorded by role. Source: `results/tables/agent_contributions.csv`. {#tbl-contributions}

### Transfer of the Optimizer's Improvements (RQ2)

The optimizer's final version reduced held-out synthetic error from 4.65 to 4.39 days, but its year-to-year agreement with MCD12Q2 on real pixels fell from 0.900 to 0.881, so it failed the entry criteria (@tbl-ablation, @fig-agent). The best version for the science was an intermediate one. Iteration 8, which stopped treating brief post-melt snowfall as dormancy, improved held-out error without losing year-to-year agreement, whereas iteration 16 traded that agreement for lower pixel bias. On held-out seasons built from real NDVI shapes, every method erred by more than 8 days, against 2–4 days on synthetic seasons, and none of the optimizer's versions moved the conclusions of the worked example.

| Version | Held-out error (days) | Annual r with MCD12Q2 |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-registered method | 4.65 | 0.900 |
| Iteration 8: ignore post-melt snow flags | 4.48 | 0.903 |
| Iteration 16: outlier-resistant amplitude | 4.40 | 0.881 |
| Final (iteration 28) | 4.39 | 0.881 |

: Kept versions of the optimizer's method on held-out and real data. {#tbl-ablation}

![Left: visible score by iteration. Right: held-out synthetic error against annual agreement with MCD12Q2 for each kept version.](../results/figures/autoresearch_dynamics.png){#fig-agent}

### Optimizer Behaviour (RQ3)

The optimizer explored five kinds of change before its first gain, kept 4 of 24 substantive attempts, and never attempted to edit another file (@fig-attempts). It also reasoned directly from the benchmark generator it was allowed to read, which 26 of its 33 rationales cite, including all three kept substantive changes. Iteration 8, for instance, was justified by noting that late snowfall occurs "in about 20% of seasons" in the generator. Once substantive ideas stopped succeeding, it kept four changes that only deleted lines to reduce the line-count penalty, and in its last five iterations it reported that no idea remained and made no edit. By iteration 16 the run had used an estimated USD 7.50 of its USD 17.90 total and achieved essentially all of its real gain.

![Each iteration by the kind of change attempted, coded from the optimizer's rationale.](../results/figures/autoresearch_attempts.png){#fig-attempts}

## Discussion

### What Can Be Gained

In this case, agents added more value by checking the research than by optimising it. The auditors prevented a biased design, corrected a misreported result, and reversed an interpretation, whereas the optimizer produced one physically reasoned idea that the science could have used. Two further gains are less obvious. First, the optimizer's 24 substantive attempts, each with a written rationale and a measured effect, amount to a documented exploration of the method's design space, which could serve as an automated sensitivity analysis if every candidate's code were saved. Next, its turn to gaming coincided with the exhaustion of its ideas, which suggests that gaming can serve as a measurable signal for stopping a search.

### What Went Wrong

There are seven main errors in how this study was run. First, the optimizer could read the benchmark generator, so it designed changes around the generator's rules, which may explain why its gains on real-shaped seasons were small. Second, the line-count penalty and the fixed penalty for failed seasons invited gaming, and the keep-if-better rule on one score discarded the version that served the science best. Next, the code of reverted candidates was not saved, so the loop's exploration cannot be re-analysed, and the loop had no stopping rule, so about USD 10.40 was spent after its real gains ended. Furthermore, the optimizer could not run code, which kept its hit rate at 17%, and the loop was run once with one model, so its behaviour cannot be separated from chance. In addition, the literature audit ran after the confirmatory analysis rather than before it, so several corrections had to be reported as deviations. The plausibility criterion for the optimizer's method was also not defined precisely in the pre-registration. The pre-registration itself was committed four seconds before the confirmatory run, within a single session, so its protection rests on the order of operations rather than on elapsed time. Lastly, the builder introduced errors that only later audits caught, and the same system that built the pipeline also coded the optimizer's iterations.

### Challenges for Agentic Research

These errors point to five challenges for anyone using agents in research. First, the evaluator defines what the agent improves, and for most scientific methods the quantity that matters, such as a trend or a driver effect, is not the quantity that is easy to score. Second, ground truth is scarce, so benchmarks tend to be synthetic, and an agent that can read how they are built will learn the benchmark rather than the world. Next, agents work faster than the safeguards designed for human researchers, so pre-registration and sequencing must be enforced in code rather than trusted to time. Furthermore, the builder's errors were confident and plausible, which means that verification, rather than generation, becomes the main cost of agentic research. Lastly, agent runs are hard to reproduce, as model versions change and outputs are not deterministic, so the ledger, the prompts, and every candidate need to be archived for others to evaluate the work.

## What to Try Next

The most informative next experiments would change one element of the design at a time, and several follow directly from the errors above. First, the evaluator could score the scientific estimand directly, by building synthetic multi-year panels with a known trend and a known driver effect and rewarding their recovery, while keeping every version that is not beaten on all objectives. Second, the same loop could be run with the benchmark generator readable and unreadable, to measure how much of the optimizer's gain comes from reading it. Next, the benchmark could be built from real ground truth, for instance by using PhenoCam or field phenology sites across the boreal and tundra zones, with whole sites held out.

The study area itself could also be varied. Running the same loop across several parks, and holding out entire parks, would test whether an agent-designed method transfers across landscapes, which is a stronger test than held-out seasons from one place. Letting the agent select its own data sources or predictors is the most tempting extension, but it carries the greatest risk, since choosing data after seeing results is the agentic equivalent of searching for significance. It should therefore be tried only if the agent proposes its choices before seeing the outcome, a human approves them, and the confirmatory test runs on held-out years or parks.

Several smaller changes would also be informative, such as giving the optimizer a sandboxed tool to test its own changes, saving every candidate so the loop doubles as a sensitivity analysis, stopping after a set number of reports that no idea remains, and comparing several models or several independent agents on the same task. Some directions, in contrast, appear less promising. These include longer runs of the same loop, which saturated by iteration 16; more powerful search on a synthetic benchmark, which was the binding constraint; penalties on line count; and any role for agents in the confirmatory test itself. Lastly, the finding that auditors contributed more than the optimizer could be tested directly, by giving auditing and optimising agents equal budgets across several studies and comparing the problems each resolves.

## Applications

For teams building agent loops, the repository's `autoresearch/` directory can be reused for any method that fits in one function with a measurable error. This study suggests scoring the scientific estimand, keeping a Pareto archive, rejecting edits that leave outputs unchanged, hiding the benchmark generator, saving every candidate, and enforcing every rule in code outside the agent. For research groups adopting agents more broadly, the case suggests running auditing agents on the plan before any code is written and on the literature before the confirmatory analysis, and keeping a record of what each agent caught. For analysts and park managers, the green-up pipeline can be applied to another park by changing `config.yaml`. In Wapusk, snow-off and April–May warmth, which were known by the end of May in 20 of 24 years, predicted mid-green-up to within about four days.

## Limitations

There are four main limitations to this research. First, it is a single case study, with one research task, one model family, and one optimizer run, so its findings are suggestive rather than general. Second, the record of contributions by role was compiled by the builder and is not exhaustive, and the coding of the optimizer's iterations was performed by the same system, so both should be treated as descriptive. Next, the costs reported are estimates at API list prices rather than billed amounts. Lastly, the worked example has its own limitations, including a short record for detecting trends and the absence of ground phenology for validation, which are documented in the repository.

## Conclusion

This study examined what coding agents contributed to a complete environmental analysis in three roles. The optimizer improved one method on held-out synthetic data, but its improvements did not carry over to the scientific result, it learned from the benchmark it could read, and it gamed its score once its ideas ran out. The auditors, in contrast, caught most of the consequential problems, including errors made by the builder. Overall, these results suggest that the near-term value of agents in research lies as much in checking work as in producing it, and that agentic research will need evaluators scored on the scientific estimand, benchmarks the agent cannot read, and safeguards enforced in code.
